segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Isha in the original: satyasya and apihitam, the face of truth under a golden lid, and a neighbor's blessing asking for a shining face. Now the Isha's last two verses.
screen: `TRUTH, UNDER A GOLDEN LID.` · `NOW: THE LAST TWO VERSES.`

segments.voice: The last text of the night is often not a goodbye. It's an ask: drive safe. Text me when you're home. So how does the Isha end, with an answer or a request? A request. No summary, no final argument. One line for the body, one line for the mind, and then a call to a fire: agne naya supatha. Agni, lead us by the good path.
screen: `TEXT ME WHEN YOU'RE HOME.` → `NOT AN ANSWER: A REQUEST.` → `AGNI, LEAD US.`

segments.voice: Verse seventeen opens with no verb at all: vayur anilam amritam. Breath, to the wind, the deathless; the reader hears goes. Then the body, ending in ash: bhasma is ash, anta is end. Then the mind: krato smara, kritam smara. Mind, remember; remember what was done. Verse eighteen calls a name: agne, Agni, the fire. Naya, lead. Supatha, by the good path, with su- meaning good. O god who knows all the ways, keep the crooked fault away from us, and take our fullest words of homage. The Isha opened with the Lord clothing, or dwelling in, all this. It closes with someone asking to be led. Now the week, held up once more. A mirror made of word order. A portrait in nots, then a poet. Iva, as it were, and what was heard from the steady ones. Two ca's carried across a river. An echo with one word changed. A golden lid. Six days of slow reading, and the same few tools each time: find the verb, undo the join, catch the ending.
screen: `BREATH TO THE WIND, BODY TO ASH.` · `SMARA: MIND, REMEMBER.` · `AGNE NAYA SUPATHA: LEAD US.` · `A WEEK OF THE ISHA, BACK IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Count back through today on your fingers: one thing you did this morning, one at midday, one just now. Let each come back plainly, without judging it: smara, remember what was done. Then rest the hands and let the counting stop.
Reading the Isha in the original, all the way to its last line: breath to the wind, the mind told to remember, and Agni asked to lead.

howItsDone: Agne naya supatha is also a Rig Vedic verse to Agni, and some Hindus recite it in daily prayers and at the fire; Shankara's commentary on the Isha explains both closing verses.
